newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan power firm bows to threat of referendum.
newsitem.headline: Japan power firm bows to threat of referendum.

text.p: A Japanese power company has scrapped a plan to build a nuclear power plant on the southern main island of Kyushu, bowing to the threat of a negative result in a referendum by residents.

A spokesman for Kyushu Electric Power Company, one of Japan's 10 power companies, said on Tuesday it has abandoned a plan to build a nuclear plant in the southern Japanese city of Kushima because of strong local opposition.
The latest decision over the proposed Kushima plant follows Japan's first local referendum held over the controversial issue of nuclear power plants.
Last August, the small town of Maki in northern Japan held a referendum on Tohoku Electric Power Company's plan to build a nuclear power plant and voters returned a majority "no" vote.
The Maki referendum was the first ever held in Japan on any subject.

Although the result was not legally binding, Maki mayor Takaaki Sasaguchi decided not to sell town land to the power firm after the vote, effectively halting Tohoku Electric's 25-year-old plan to build a nuclear plant there.
The Maki referendum came after decades of ambitious and often controversial construction of nuclear plants by Japanese power companies. A third of Japan's power needs are supplied by nuclear plants.
Media reports said Kyushu Electric decided to scrap the Kushima plan because it expected a majority of residents would vote against the plan in a referendum planned for the summer.
A city official said the vote would be held as scheduled, despite the power firm's decision.
